title: Reading Maketh a Full Man
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "Of Studies," in The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral by Francis Bacon (1625).
body: STUDIES serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability. Their chief use for delight, is in privateness and retiring; for ornament, is in discourse; and for ability, is in the judgment, and disposition of business. For expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best, from those that are learned. To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament, is affectation; to make judgment wholly by their rules, is the humor of a scholar. They perfect nature, and are perfected by experience: for natural abilities are like natural plants, that need proyning, by study; and studies themselves, do give forth directions too much at large, except they be bounded in by experience.

Crafty men contemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them; for they teach not their own use; but that is a wisdom without them, and above them, won by observation. Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider. Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention.

Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. And therefore, if a man write little, he had need have a great memory; if he confer little, he had need have a present wit: and if he read little, he had need have much cunning, to seem to know, that he doth not. Histories make men wise; poets witty; the mathematics subtile; natural philosophy deep; moral grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what are the three chief uses of studies?
Per the passage, what does the author call spending too much time in studies?
According to the passage, what does reading make a man, according to the author?
Per the passage, what does the author say writing makes a man?
Based on the passage, why does the author say a man who writes little needs a great memory?
options: Without writing things down, he must rely on memory to retain what he has learned
Writing was considered a sign of poor memory in itself
Memory and writing were thought to be entirely unrelated skills
A great memory was required before one could learn to write

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author compare natural abilities to plants that need "proyning" (pruning) by study?
options: Natural talent alone is unrefined and needs the shaping discipline of study to reach its full potential
Plants and human minds require the exact same care
Study can only harm natural talent, not improve it
Pruning was a common hobby among scholars of the time

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author warn against making judgment "wholly by their rules"?
options: Relying entirely on the rules found in books, rather than one's own judgment, is a narrow, overly bookish habit of mind
Books contain no useful rules at all
Rules from books were considered illegal to follow
Judgment should never be informed by books in any way

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say some books should be "tasted" while others should be "chewed and digested"?
options: Different books deserve different levels of attention depending on their importance and depth
All books should be read exactly the same way
Only bad books should be read quickly
Chewing and digesting refers to literally destroying old books

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Studies are valuable for several purposes, but must be balanced with experience and read with judgment rather than followed blindly
Studies are useless without a formal teacher
Only the wealthy should pursue serious study
Reading is inferior to writing in every respect

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that using studies too much for ornament is "affectation"?
options: An artificial display meant to impress rather than a genuine trait
A natural and sincere expression of learning

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who does the author say condemns studies?
Per the passage, what does the author say conference (conversation) makes a man?
According to the passage, what subject does the author say makes men "witty"?
Per the passage, what should a reader do instead of reading "to contradict and confute"?
Based on the passage, why does the author say true wisdom about using studies comes from "observation" rather than from the studies themselves?
options: Books can inform the mind but cannot teach a person how or when to apply that knowledge in life
Studies are entirely useless compared to observation
Observation is simply another word for reading
Only uneducated people rely on observation

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the author's advice on reading books of differing importance?
options: Readers should adjust their attention to match each book's value, some deserving only a taste and others careful digestion
All books deserve exactly the same careful attention
Only short books are worth reading at all
Books should be judged solely by their length

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that mathematics makes men "subtile"?
